card: Paper card. Question: Can a Ti–Zr–Nb–Ta–Ag high-entropy alloy (HEA) processed via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS) exhibit superior mechanical properties and corrosion resistance in artificial saliva compared to commercial Ti6Al4V for dental implant applications?. System: Ti–Zr–Nb–Ta–Ag HEA (35% Ti, 35% Zr, 20% Nb, 5% Ta, 5% Ag atomic %) and commercial Ti6Al4V. Processing: High-energy ball milling (300 rpm, 20 h, WC vials/balls, argon atmosphere) followed by spark plasma sintering (1200 °C, 50 MPa, 10 min, 200 °C/min heating rate, vacuum ~5 × 10⁻² mbar). Test conditions: In vitro corrosion tests in artificial saliva (Fusayama–Meyer type) at pH 3.0, 4.9, and 6.8; microindentation (100 mN load); electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (1 kHz to 1 mHz); potentiodynamic polarization (+250 mV to −2000 mV vs Ag/AgCl); XPS; contact angle measurements. Findings: The SPS-processed HEA exhibited a hardness of 8.2 GPa, nearly double that of Ti6Al4V (4.11 GPa).; The resistance to plastic deformation (H³/E²) for the HEA was 0.0312 GPa, significantly higher than 0.00349 GPa for Ti6Al4V.; The HEA showed the highest charge transfer resistance (Rct) of 1.0805 × 10⁷ Ω⋅cm² at pH 6.8, compared to Ti6Al4V.; The double-layer constant phase element (CPEdl) value for the HEA was 0.085 µF⁻¹⋅cm⁻²⋅sⁿ, indicating a more stable passive film.; Corrosion current density (icorr) for the HEA declined by at least one order of magnitude compared to Ti6Al4V at all pH levels.; XPS analysis confirmed the formation of biocompatible surface oxides including TiO₂, ZrO₂, Nb₂O₅, Ta₂O₅, and metallic Ag.; The HEA surface was moderately hydrophobic with a contact angle of 83.9° for water, compared to 65.41° for Ti6Al4V.; The HEA microstructure consisted of dual BCC phases (BCC1, BCC2) and an ultrafine Zr-based phase with crystallite sizes of 21.7 nm, 15.8 nm, and 23 nm respectively.. Mechanism: The superior mechanical properties are attributed to refined microstructure, multicomponent alloying effects, solid-solution strengthening, and grain boundary strengthening resulting from severe plastic deformation during ball milling and controlled recrystallization during SPS. The enhanced corrosion resistance is due to the formation of a compact, inert, and stable passive film composed of TiO₂, ZrO₂, Nb₂O₅, and Ta₂O₅, which effectively impedes charge transfer and protects the matrix, particularly in acidic environments where Ti6Al4V films degrade.. Limitations: The elastic modulus of the HEA (~132 GPa) is slightly higher than commercially pure titanium (~110 GPa), which may lead to stress shielding, although it is lower than Co–Cr and stainless steel alloys.. Future work: Future work should focus on optimizing the elastic modulus and reducing potential stress shielding through compositional adjustments (e.g., increasing β-phase stabilizing elements) and introducing controlled porosity via advanced processing strategies.. Quote: "The HEA exhibits nearly double the hardness (8.2 GPa) and significantly higher resistance to plastic deformation (H³/E² =0.0312 GPa) compared to Ti6Al4V"

Paper card. Question: To evaluate the potential of a Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Ag high entropy alloy synthesized via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering for dental bioimplant applications, specifically regarding its phase composition, microstructure, mechanical properties, surface characteristics, and corrosion resistance.. System: Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Ag high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Mechanical alloying followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS). Test conditions: In vitro corrosion testing in artificial saliva at acidic pH; microhardness measurement; XPS surface characterization. Findings: The SPS process resulted in a homogeneous microstructure with dual phases: BCC structure and an equiaxed Zr-rich phase.; The microhardness of the SPS-ed HEA was 8.2 GPa, nearly double that of Ti6Al4V (4.11 GPa).; XPS analysis revealed the formation of surface oxides including TiO2, ZrO2, Nb2O5, and Ta2O5 alongside Ag.; The SPSed HEA outperformed Ti6Al4V in corrosion resistance in artificial saliva, showing higher impedance values and lower corrosion current densities even at acidic pH.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the suitability of the material to the combination of its mechanical strength (derived from the dual-phase microstructure) and enhanced in vitro corrosion resistance (due to the formation of protective surface oxides).. Future work: Future studies should focus on the in vivo evaluation and long-term performance assessment of the developed HEA under real oral conditions.. Quote: "This study reports the synthesis of Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Ag HEA via mechanical alloying and SPS and evaluates its potential for dental bioimplant applications."

card: Paper card. Question: To evaluate the biocompatibility of Ti-6Al-4V alloy powder by determining its effects on behavior, blood chemistry, and antioxidant profiles in vital organs of albino mice after short-term exposure.. System: Ti-6Al-4V alloy powder (6% aluminum and 4% vanadium by weight, >99.9% purity constituents). Processing: Melting in an electric arc furnace under 10−5 mbar vacuum with argon gas, repeated four times for homogeneity; homogenized at 1100 °C in vacuum for 8 h; powder prepared for gavage at 25 mg/ml solvent/Kg body weight. Test conditions: Oral gavage for 8 days; behavioral tests (rota rod, open field, novel object, light-dark box); analysis of complete blood count, serum parameters, and antioxidant metabolites (SOD, catalase, lipid peroxidation) in liver, heart, lungs, kidney, and brain. Findings: Rota rod test performance significantly decreased in male mice (P = 0.05) compared to control.; Novel object recognition capability significantly reduced in female mice (P = 0.04) compared to control.; Superoxide dismutase (SOD) concentration significantly elevated in liver (P = 0.008), heart (P = 0.01), and lungs (P = 0.05) of female mice.; Catalase concentration significantly decreased in liver (P = 0.001) of female mice.; SOD concentration in lungs significantly reduced (P = 0.05) in male mice.; Body weight, complete blood count, and serum parameters remained unaffected in both genders.; Open field, light-dark box, and other antioxidant parameters varied non-significantly (P > 0.05).. Mechanism: The alloy powder crosses the blood-brain barrier to affect brain functioning, and the observed changes in antioxidant enzymes (SOD and catalase) reflect disturbed H₂O₂ associated metabolic pathways and increased H₂O₂ production in cells due to ROS formation from metal corrosion or ion release.. Limitations: The exposure time of 8 days may not have been long enough to disturb blood chemistry, and the study was limited to a single dose (25 mg/ml solvent/Kg body weight).. Future work: Effects must be extensively explored under variable dose and exposure time conditions to know more about their biocompatibility.. Quote: "Short tern exposure to Ti 6Al 4V powder drastically affected neuromuscular coordination in male mice during rota rod test."

card: Paper card. Question: How can single-phase, chemically homogeneous high-entropy borides be synthesized using mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering, and how do composition and sintering temperature affect their microstructure, hardness, and thermal-oxidative resistance?. System: TiZrHfNbTa borides (specifically equiatomic (TiZrHfTaNb)B2 and non-equiatomic (TiTaNb)0.3Hf0.35Zr0.35B2). Processing: Mechanical alloying of elemental metal powders (Ti, Nb, Hf, Zr, Ta) in a Fritsch Pulverisette 4 planetary mill (200–400 rpm, 7.5 h) followed by mixing with polycrystalline boron (1:2 molar ratio) and spark plasma sintering (50 MPa, 5 min hold) at 1600, 1800, or 2000 °C. Test conditions: Microhardness measured at 300 and 500 g; gas-dynamic tests using an electric arc plasma torch (UPIM-200) with heat flux density ranging from 3.11 to 4.2 MW/m2 in an air plasma-forming gas. Findings: A chemically homogeneous powder with low iron content (0.12%) was obtained after 7.5 h of mechanical alloying at 200–400 rpm.; Single-phase hexagonal MeB2 structure (P63/mmc) was formed during spark plasma sintering at 2000 °C.; Microhardness values ranged from 1763 to 1959 HV, with the highest hardness (1959 HV) observed at 1600 °C due to non-equilibrium phases.; Increasing sintering temperature to 2000 °C reduced oxide inclusions and increased chemical homogeneity.; The maximum test temperature without intensive entrainment and melting was 1904 °C for the equiatomic sample and 2070 °C for the Hf/Zr-enriched sample.; The liquid phase appeared on the surface at approximately 1815 °C for the equiatomic sample and 1910 °C for the Hf/Zr-enriched sample.; Layer-by-layer analysis revealed a surface layer of mixed refractory MeO2 dioxide and a third layer containing low-melting Me4O5 oxides.. Mechanism: The formation of high-entropy borides during sintering is accompanied by large heat releases, inducing self-propagating high-temperature synthesis where particles melt and redox reactions occur in parallel. The presence of hafnium and zirconium oxides is attributed to the lowest free energy of their formation. Increasing temperature accelerates diffusion, leading to the coagulation and dissolution of oxide inclusions, while boron oxide evaporation and interaction with tooling carbon at temperatures above 1860 °C and 2000 °C further reduce oxide phases. The enhanced thermal-oxidative resistance in Hf/Zr-rich compositions is due to the formation of a surface layer enriched in refractory Zr and Hf oxides.. Limitations: The text notes that the initial power for gas-dynamic tests was chosen approximately due to a lack of prior data on material characteristics. Additionally, the presence of a halo in diffraction patterns at 1800 °C indicates the persistence of an X-ray amorphous fine-grained ceramic component.. Future work: The authors state that increasing the temperature or holding time during sintering will likely lead to the complete dissolution of oxide phases.. Quote: "A chemically homogeneous powder with a low iron content (0.12%) was obtained in a planetary mill by rotating the planetary disk/pots at 200–400 rpm and a processing time of 7.5 h."
